c01|3.answer_text: The operating‑margin shift was the result of several offsetting items.  In 2018 the margin fell 2.3 percentage points versus 2017, driven primarily by: • A gain on the May 2017 divestiture of the identity‑management business, which reduced the margin; • Higher defined‑benefit pension, post‑retirement service‑cost and defined‑contribution expenses, which also pulled the margin down; • Acquisition impacts (mainly the Scott Safety purchase) and lower divestiture gains (excluding the identity‑management and Communication‑Markets sales) that further decreased the margin; • Remaining stranded costs from the Communication‑Markets divestiture that reduced the margin; • Conversely, organic local‑currency growth, productivity improvements and lower portfolio and supply‑chain footprint‑optimization charges lifted the margin; • The loss of lower‑margin operating income from businesses that were divested added a positive contribution.  The net effect of these opposing forces was the 2.3‑point margin decline.

c06|2.answer_text: The 10‑K filings describe inventory as a key balance‑sheet item that is valued at the lower of cost (often FIFO or average cost) or net realizable value. Companies emphasize the need to forecast demand accurately; under‑estimates can cause shortages, while over‑estimates can lead to excess inventory that may become obsolete and require write‑downs or write‑offs. Inventory reserves are regularly reviewed and adjusted based on assumptions about future demand, market conditions, historical sales, and product life‑cycle status. Excess or obsolete inventory is written down to its estimated net realizable value, and shrinkage reserves are estimated from historical loss percentages. These policies are intended to prevent material impacts on gross profit or operating income.
